question: How old is a kidney tumor of a given size, i.e. what is the distribution of age conditioned on size?
contributions: A simple constant-doubling-time calculation answering the veteran's question
A Monte Carlo growth simulation that builds the joint distribution of age and size and slices it to get p(age|size)
A sensitivity check for serial correlation in growth rate and for non-spherical geometry

results.claim: At the median growth rate, the 15.5 cm tumor would have been about 6 cm at discharge, so it probably formed before discharge.
results.setup: Interval discharge to diagnosis 3291 days; median volume doubling time 811 days (Zhang et al); linear doubling time = 3x volume doubling time; final diameter 15.5 cm.
results.quote: The result, d0, is about 6 cm.

results.claim: If the tumor started at 0.1 cm after discharge it needs 7.3 linear doublings, implying RDT 2.4, which only 20% of observed tumors reached.
results.setup: Initial linear size 0.1 cm, final 15.5 cm, interval 3291 days; compared with Zhang et al growth rates.
results.quote: The number of doublings, in linear measure, is 7.3, which implies an RDT of 2.4.

results.claim: Only 20% of tumors in the Zhang et al data grew as fast as RDT 2.4.
results.setup: Zhang et al untreated renal tumors, serial CT; data read off a printed graph.
results.quote: In the data from Zhang et al, only 20% of tumors grew this fast during a period of observation.

results.claim: With no serial correlation, a 15.5 cm tumor is older than 8 years with probability 0.999.
results.setup: Simulated joint distribution of age and size; uncorrelated growth rates; spherical geometry.
results.quote: With no serial correlation, the probability that a 15.5 cm tumor is older than 8 years is 0.999, or almost certain.

results.claim: With serial correlation 0.4 the probability is 0.995 and with 0.8 it is 0.978.
results.setup: As above, with target correlation rho between successive growth rates.
results.quote: With correlation 0.4, faster-growing tumors are more likely, but the probability is still 0.995. Even with correlation 0.8, the probability is 0.978.

results.claim: If the 15.5 x 15 cm tumor is flat with the volume of a 6 cm sphere and rho is 0.8, P(age > 8 years) is still 95%.
results.setup: Volume equal to a 6 cm sphere; correlation 0.8.
results.quote: With this smaller volume and correlation 0.8, the probability of age greater than 8 is still 95%.

results.claim: For a 6 cm tumor, serial correlation 0.4 widens the age range; the 95th percentile of age rises from 30.2 to 36.9 years.
results.table: Table 13.1, row serial correlation 0.4, diameter 6.0, column 95th

results.claim: Fastest simulated tumors reach 10 cm in 8 years, slowest take more than 35.
results.quote: the fastest-growing tumor gets there in 8 years; the slowest takes more than 35.

results.claim: Generating 10000 values at rho=0.4 through the CDF transform gives an actual correlation of 0.37.

limits: Spherical-tumor assumption is probably not valid for very large tumors.
Growth-rate distribution is fit to only 53 patients, data read from a printed graph (raw data refused); a larger sample would give a different distribution.
No dependence on subtype, grade or size; growth rate chosen independently each interval apart from the rho variant; true serial correlation unknown.
Extrapolates beyond observed sizes of 1.0 to 12.0 cm (simulation runs 0.3 to 20 cm).
Python 2 era code using the thinkbayes module; code listings have missing arguments (Cache.Add called with rdt but defined without it).
practices: Start with a simple model and use it to validate a more complex one (13.2).
When p(size|age) is easy to simulate but p(age|size) is not, simulate the joint distribution and slice it instead of applying Bayes's theorem explicitly (13.8).
Test each modeling assumption for sensitivity, here serial correlation and geometry (13.7).
Use a Gaussian copula style transform (correlated Gaussian, Gaussian CDF, inverse of target CDF) to generate correlated draws from any marginal (13.7).
